content: Matricaria is a genus of flowering plants that belongs to the sunflower family, Asteraceae. Some species within this genus are commonly referred to as mayweed, although this name is also applied to plants outside of the Matricaria genus. These plants are predominantly found in temperate regions of Europe, Asia, and the Americas, as well as in parts of northern and southern Africa. Certain species have also become naturalized in Australia. While Matricaria occidentalis is native to North America, other species have been introduced to the region. These plants are hardy annuals with a pleasant aromatic quality. They typically grow in nutrient-rich fallow lands, along roadsides, and in ruderal habitats. Despite being considered nuisance weeds by some, they are well-suited for use in rock gardens, herb gardens, and as border plants. The stems of Matricaria species are highly branched, ranging from prostrate to erect, and are smooth and densely leafy. Their bipinnate leaves are composed of numerous narrow, linear lobes. The flowers of Matricaria are radially symmetrical. The greenish-yellow capitula are semi-spherical in shape. Some species, such as Matricaria recutita, have white ray florets, while others, like Matricaria discoidea, lack them. The disc florets are characterized by having four to five teeth. The receptacle of the flower is two to three times taller than it is wide. The pappus, if present, is short and crown-shaped, though it may also be absent. Matricaria species serve as food plants for the larvae of certain Lepidoptera species, including the Lime-speck Pug moth. The extract of German chamomile (Matricaria recutita) is commonly consumed as a strong tea. This extract has been traditionally used in herbal medicine for its carminative (gas-relieving) and anti-inflammatory properties. Additionally, it is incorporated into ointments, lotions, and mouthwashes to treat infections of the mouth and gums. In aromatherapy, two essential oils derived from chamomile are widely used. These include true chamomile oil, also known as German chamomile oil, which is extracted from Matricaria recutita, and Roman chamomile oil, which is obtained from Anthemis nobilis. The taxonomy of the Matricaria genus is a subject of ongoing debate and confusion. Some species are classified under the genus Tripleurospermum rather than Matricaria, depending on the interpretation of the author. The distinction between these two genera is based on the number of seed ribs: Tripleurospermum species have one adaxial and two lateral seed ribs, whereas Matricaria species possess four or five adaxial seed ribs.
